newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania to deploy troops as crisis mounts.
newsitem.headline: Albania to deploy troops as crisis mounts.

text.p: Albania's parliament handed President Sali Berisha special powers to restore order on Sunday after demonstrators clashed with riot police in Tirana and set scores of buildings ablaze in towns across the Balkan state.

Parliament, sitting for the first time on a Sunday since the ruling right-wing Democratic Party swept to power in a 1992 general election, voted at a crisis session to give Berisha the power to deploy troops to unblock roads and guard government buildings.

"This decision has nothing to do with a state of emergency but the traffic, water depots, oil reserves, town halls...and strategic sites should not be attacked," Foreign Minister Tritan Shehuhe told Reuters after the meeting.
Soldiers armed with sub-machine guns were already on alert in central Tirana, stationed around ministries and other strategic points in the Albanian capital.

The emergency measures were agreed after thousands of demonstrators in Tirana clashed with riot police, who used batons and water cannon to disperse crowds angry over the collapse of pyramid savings schemes.
Albanian television showed aerial pictures of disturbances in some 13 other towns where protesters torched town halls, courts and offices of the ruling Democrats.
Violence over the weekend was the worst seen in Albania since 1991, when some 40 people were killed in food riots.
Around 30,000 people converged in central Tirana on Sunday calling on the government of Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi to resign over its handling of the pyramid schemes.

Police fired their pistols in the air over the din of shouts and screams as a hard core of around 3,000 protesters tried to advance towards parliament, smashing the windows of the Palace of Culture in the central Skanderbeg Square.
"Down with Berisha!", "Down with Meksi!", "Down with the thieves!", demonstrators shouted.

The crowd dispersed after the clashes. One of Tirana's three main hospitals said it had treated seven demonstrators and seven police officers. Three protesters remained in hospital, one of them in intensive care, a duty doctor said.

Leaders of the main opposition parties, who boycotted a general election last May and have refused to take up the handful of seats allocated to them in parliament, called for Sunday's demonstrations but urged participants to be peaceful.
The main opposition Socialist Party, heirs to the former communists, demanded the creation of an interim government of experts ahead of a new general election.

Meksi said on Sunday that people who had invested in some collapsing schemes would be repaid from February 5, but it was unclear whether the government had enough money at its disposal to satisfy impoverished Albanians fearing complete ruin.
Some 84 police officers were injured in Sunday's clashes, some of them seriously, but there were no official figures for protesters hurt in the demonstrations.

Albanian state television showed pictures of the town of Korca, 180 km (110 miles) southeast of Tirana near the border with Greece, where smoke billowed out of the burnt-out headquarters of the local Democratic Party.

In Berat, 120 km (75 miles) south of the capital, protesters set fire to the court and offices of the state prosecutor. Government and Democratic Party buildings were also burnt in the southwestern towns of Fier and Vlore.
Shehu blamed the crisis on "extremist forces".
"It is not the mass of Albanian Socialists, but there are some Marxist extremists who have always wanted to seize power through violence," he said.
"These are segments of the former secret police who want to profit from this moment when Albanian citizens are having financial difficulties to try to destabilise Albania."
